Figure gallery: everyone shows their best figure at once.
activities.tagline: A loop of string, ten fingers, endless figures.

variations.easier: Learn just the opening position and invent your own figures.
variations.harder: Chain figures: transfer a figure through three partners in a row.

activities.name: Measure the Pumpkin
activities.tagline: Circumference, weight, seed guesses — a pumpkin turns into a math lab.

materials.item: pumpkins in a few different sizes (one per small group)

activities.setup: Set out one pumpkin per small group with a tape measure and a recording sheet (columns: guess / actual for circumference, weight, seed count).
steps: Each group predicts: how many inches around their pumpkin, how heavy it is, and how many seeds are inside. Write every guess down first — no measuring yet.
Measure the circumference at the widest point with the tape measure. Record the actual number next to the guess.
Weigh the pumpkin. Compare — who guessed closest?
Estimate the seed count. Then the teacher cuts the pumpkin open (adults only on the knife) and each group scoops and counts their pumpkin's seeds in piles of ten.
Compare seed counts: does the biggest pumpkin hold the most seeds? Usually not — great discussion starter.

variations.easier: Skip the seed count and just do circumference and weight predictions.
variations.harder: Graph every group's results and look for patterns between size, weight, and seed count.

activities.safety: Only the adult handles the knife when opening pumpkins. Wash hands after handling seeds and pulp.

activities.name: Pumpkin Seed Sprouting Baggies
activities.tagline: Seeds wake up on the classroom window — watch germination happen day by day.

materials.item: pumpkin seeds (saved from a carved pumpkin or a seed packet)

activities.setup: Dampen the paper towels (wring out the drips). Give each kid a bag, a towel, and 3–4 seeds.
steps: Fold the damp paper towel and slide it into the bag with 3–4 seeds pressed against the towel so you can see them.
Seal the bag and tape it to a sunny window — the bag is its own little greenhouse.
Each day, kids observe and draw what they see: nothing, a crack, a root, a sprout.
After a week, compare: which seeds sprouted first? Did seeds near the top of the bag beat the ones at the bottom?
Transplant the best sprouts into cups of soil if you want a longer project.

variations.easier: Sprout just one seed per bag so it's easy to watch.
variations.harder: Run a side experiment: one bag in the dark, one in the light — compare the sprouts.

activities.name: Apple Browning Lab
activities.tagline: Why do cut apples turn brown? Kids run the experiment and find out.

materials.item: kid-safe knives or pre-sliced apple wedges

activities.setup: Slice each apple into 4 wedges (adults slice, or hand out pre-cut wedges). Set out cups labeled: plain water, lemon-juice water, salt water, nothing.
steps: Soak one wedge in each liquid for 2 minutes. Leave one wedge untouched on a plate.
Line all four wedges up and predict: which will stay the freshest-looking after 20 minutes?
Wait. Do another activity or read aloud while the clock runs.
Compare the wedges. The lemon-juice one usually stays pale — the acid slows the browning reaction.
Taste test (optional): does the protected wedge taste different? Discuss what 'browning' actually is — air reacting with the apple's flesh.

variations.easier: Test just two treatments: lemon juice vs. nothing.
variations.harder: Try more treatments (vinegar, honey water, milk) and have kids design the experiment themselves, including a control.

activities.safety: Check for fruit allergies first, and have everyone wash hands before and after handling food.

activities.name: Fall Leaf Chromatography
activities.tagline: Hidden colors inside fall leaves separate out on a coffee filter.
activities.setup: An adult pours a half-inch of rubbing alcohol into each jar. Give each group leaves, a filter strip, and a pencil.
steps: Tear the leaves into small pieces and drop them into the jar so they're covered by the alcohol.
Let the jar sit 10–15 minutes, swirling now and then — the alcohol pulls the leaf's pigments out.
Cut a strip of coffee filter, tape it to a pencil, and rest the pencil across the jar so the strip's tip just touches the liquid.
Wait 20–30 minutes. The liquid climbs the strip and the hidden colors (yellows, oranges, even greens) separate into bands.
Dry the strips and compare: do red leaves and yellow leaves hide the same colors?

variations.easier: Do one jar as a whole-class demo instead of per-group jars.
variations.harder: Test leaves from different trees and sort the dried strips into a class color chart.

activities.safety: Rubbing alcohol is adult-handled only, and jars stay on the table — no carrying them around. Work in a ventilated room.

activities.name: Leaf Animal Collage
activities.tagline: Dry leaves become foxes, owls, and hedgehogs — nature's sticker book.

materials.item: a basket of dry fall leaves in different shapes and colors

activities.setup: Spread the leaves out on a table so kids can browse shapes. Hand out cardstock and glue.
steps: Sort through the leaves: which ones look like ears? A round body? A pointy tail?
Lay out an animal on the paper WITHOUT gluing first — arrange, step back, adjust.
Glue the pieces down one at a time, biggest pieces first.
Add details with markers or googly eyes: faces, legs, whiskers.
Title the piece and hang a class 'leaf zoo' gallery.

variations.easier: Glue pre-cut leaf shapes onto a printed animal outline.
variations.harder: Make a whole habitat scene — the animal plus leaf trees, sun, and ground.

activities.name: Paper-Bag Ghost Puppets
activities.tagline: Lunch bags + tissue paper = a cast of friendly ghosts for a puppet show.

materials.item: white tissue paper or crepe streamers

activities.setup: Set out bags with the flat bottom facing up — that flat square is the ghost's face.
steps: Draw a silly (not scary) ghost face on the flat bottom of the bag: big round eyes, an 'o' mouth.
Cut or tear tissue paper into strips and glue them around the bag's opening — these are the ghost's flowy bottom.
Slide a hand inside and practice: ghosts bob, spin, and say 'booo' in a friendly voice.
Pair up and improvise a 2-minute ghost puppet scene behind a desk 'stage'.
Perform for the class. Applaud every ghost.

variations.easier: Skip the tissue strips — just decorate and perform with the bag.
variations.harder: Write a short script for the ghost scene and perform it with simple props.

activities.name: Handprint Bat Garland
activities.tagline: Two handprints make bat wings — string them into a classroom garland.
activities.setup: Cut black paper into pieces big enough for two handprints. Put out white crayons for tracing.
steps: Trace both hands on the black paper — fingers spread wide. These are the bat's wings.
Cut out the hands (younger kids: an adult helps with scissors).
Cut a small oval for the body and two triangle ears; glue them between the wings.
Draw a friendly face with the white crayon.
String everyone's bats onto yarn and hang the garland across the room.

variations.easier: The teacher pre-cuts handprint pairs; kids just decorate and string them.
variations.harder: Add a research card to each bat: one real bat fact (they eat insects, they hang upside down).

activities.safety: Scissors stay at the table and cut paper only — adults help the youngest cutters.

activities.name: Spiderweb Plate Weaving
activities.tagline: Weave yarn across a paper plate into a web, then add a spider.
activities.setup: Punch 10–12 holes evenly around each plate's rim. Cut the center out of the plates so only the rim ring remains (adults do the center cut).
steps: Tie yarn through one hole with a knot to anchor it.
Weave across the plate: through one hole, across the middle, out another hole — crisscross until a web forms.
Tie off the end with a knot and trim the tail.
Add a spider: a plastic ring spider, or make one from a pom-pom with pipe-cleaner legs.
Hang the webs from the ceiling with string.

variations.easier: Use pre-punched rims and shorter yarn pieces; the teacher helps with knots.
variations.harder: Weave a pattern (over-two, under-one) and add a second color for a spiral effect.

activities.safety: Adults cut the plate centers — rims tear easily, so go slow.

activities.name: Papel Picado Banners
activities.tagline: Fold and snip tissue paper into the colorful cut-paper banners of Día de los Muertos.
activities.setup: Cut tissue paper into rectangles (about 8x10 inches). Stack 3–4 sheets to cut several at once. Set out string for the finished banner.
steps: Fold the tissue rectangle in half, then in half again — small folds make detailed cuts.
Cut shapes out of the folded edges: triangles, half-circles, diamonds. Don't cut the fold completely apart.
Unfold carefully to reveal the design — every banner looks different.
Tape the top edge of each finished panel to the string, spacing them out.

Hang the banner up. Share what you know: papel picado are the festive cut-paper banners made in Mexico for Día de los Muertos — we're practicing the craft with respect for the tradition it comes from.

variations.easier: Cut simpler shapes (just triangles along one edge) on fewer folded layers.
variations.harder: Design a panel with a specific symbol — a marigold, a skull, a heart — and learn what it represents.

activities.safety: Scissors cut paper only. Tissue tears easily, so unfold slowly.

activities.name: Egg Carton Spiders
activities.tagline: One egg-carton cup + pipe-cleaner legs = a spider that actually dangles.
activities.setup: An adult cuts the cartons into single cups ahead of time — one cup per kid. Set out paint and let cups dry before decorating.
steps: Paint or color the cup black (or any spider color you like).
Poke 8 pipe-cleaner legs through the sides — 4 on each side — and bend the ends into little feet.
Glue on googly eyes. Give your spider a name.
Tie a string to the top and hang the spiders around the room — a whole spider drop.
Optional: write one true spider fact on a tag and hang it with your spider.

variations.easier: Skip the paint — decorate the cup with markers instead.
variations.harder: Build a spiderweb from yarn between two chairs and hang the whole class's spiders in it.

activities.safety: Adults cut the cartons — the cardboard is stiff. Wash hands after painting.

activities.name: Corn Husk Dolls
activities.tagline: Soak, bundle, and tie dried corn husks into old-fashioned dolls.

materials.item: dried corn husks (craft store or grocery)

activities.setup: Soak the corn husks in warm water for 10 minutes so they're bendable. Give each kid 6–8 husks and a length of twine.
steps: Lay 4 husks flat and tie them together in the middle — this bundle is the body.
Fold the top half down over the tie to make the head; tie again just below to form the neck.
Take 2 more husks, roll them tight, and tie both ends — these are the arms. Slip them through the body bundle and tie at the waist.
Arrange the bottom husks into a skirt shape and tie at the waist.
Draw a face with markers, or leave it blank like traditional husk dolls. Name your doll.

variations.easier: Make a simple version: one bundle tied for the head, one tie for the waist — no separate arms.
variations.harder: Dress the dolls with extra husk layers, tiny hats, or woven belts.

activities.safety: Soak water can be slippery — wipe up spills so nobody slips.

activities.name: Apple Print Painting
activities.tagline: Halved apples become stamps — print rows of apple patterns.
activities.setup: An adult halves the apples top-to-bottom (the star-shaped core shows) and crosswise (the round center shows). Pour paint onto plates.
steps: Look at the cut apple — spot the star in the middle.
Press the cut side into the paint, then stamp it firmly onto the paper. Lift straight up.
Make patterns: rows of stars, alternating colors, a border frame.
Try stamping with the crosswise half for a different shape.
Sign your print and let it dry flat.

variations.easier: Stamp with one color only and make a simple row pattern.
variations.harder: Carve a simple shape into the apple half with a plastic knife (adult supervises) for a custom stamp.

activities.safety: Adults do all the apple cutting. Smocks on — paint washes out of hands, not always out of shirts.

activities.name: Ghost Footprint Keepsakes
activities.tagline: One painted footprint, flipped upside down, becomes a little ghost.

materials.item: baby wipes or a damp towel

activities.setup: Pour white paint into trays. Lay out cardstock — one sheet per kid. Keep wipes handy; this one is gloriously messy.
steps: Paint the bottom of one foot white (a grown-up helper can do this part).
Press the foot firmly onto the dark paper, heel at the top — then lift straight up.
Wipe the foot clean right away.
Once dry, flip the paper so the toes point down: the footprint is now a ghost's flowy body.
Draw two eyes and a round 'boo' mouth with the black marker.

variations.easier: Do handprints instead of footprints — less wiggly.
variations.harder: Make a whole haunted-house scene around the ghost with crayons.

activities.safety: Use washable paint only, and wipe feet immediately — wet paint + tile floors are slippery.

activities.name: Fall Scavenger Bingo
activities.tagline: A bingo card full of fall — hunt the outdoors for every square.

materials.item: printed fall bingo cards (or blank cards kids draw themselves)

activities.setup: Print bingo cards with fall finds (red leaf, acorn, pinecone, yellow leaf, smooth rock, feather, piece of bark, something round, a seed, a stick shaped like a letter) — or have kids draw their own 3x3 grids and fill in fall items.
steps: Hand out a card and pencil to each kid (or pair).
Walk the yard, field, or trail together. When you spot a square's item, mark it — look, don't always pick.
First row, column, or diagonal filled = BINGO. Keep walking for a full-card blackout if energy allows.
End in a circle: each kid shows their favorite find and says why they picked it.
Leave everything where it belongs — the next class gets the same hunt.

variations.easier: Use a 3x3 card with pictures instead of words for younger kids.
variations.harder: Add a tally challenge: count how many of each item the whole group found and graph it.

activities.safety: Set clear boundaries for the walk area first. Watch for poison ivy, thorns, and busy paths.

activities.name: Build-a-Scarecrow
activities.tagline: Stuff old clothes with straw and raise a guardian for the school garden.

materials.item: a wooden stake or broom handle

activities.setup: Gather stuffing material and clothes. Pick the scarecrow's post — garden bed, playground corner, or field edge — and pound the stake in first.
steps: Stuff the shirt with straw and tie the cuffs and bottom shut with twine.
Stuff the pants the same way and tie the ankles.
Draw a face on the pillowcase, stuff it lightly, and tie it closed for the head.
Dress the scarecrow: shirt over the stake, pants tied on, head pinned at the top, hat on.
Give your scarecrow a name and a job description. Vote on the name if there are rival ideas.

variations.easier: Build a mini tabletop scarecrow from a paper bag and shredded paper instead.
variations.harder: Write a 'day in the life' story from the scarecrow's point of view.

activities.safety: Straw can be scratchy — no throwing it, and watch for kids with hay allergies.

activities.name: Leaf Collect & Sort
activities.tagline: Every kid collects ten leaves, then the group sorts them like real scientists.

materials.item: a bag or basket per kid
sorting trays, paper plates, or big sheets of paper

activities.setup: Set a collection boundary and a time limit (10 minutes). Hand out bags.
steps: Everyone collects exactly 10 different leaves — different is the goal.
Dump them out and sort them into groups. The rule is yours to invent: by color, by size, by smooth vs. jagged edges.
Count each group and lay the leaves out as a living bar graph.
Each kid explains their sorting rule to a partner. Try someone else's rule on your leaves — does it still work?
Pick the most surprising leaf and sketch it with three labeled features.

variations.easier: Collect 5 leaves and sort by one rule: color.
variations.harder: Press the most interesting leaves between book pages and start a class leaf herbarium with labels.

activities.safety: Check the area for hazards before collecting. No tasting leaves.

activities.name: Scarecrow Dress-Up Relay
activities.tagline: Sprint, dress like a scarecrow, strike a pose, sprint back — tag, you're it.

materials.item: 2 full sets of oversized clothes (flannel shirt, baggy pants, hat, gloves)
2 chairs or cones to mark the dressing stations

activities.setup: Split into two teams. At the far end, set out one full scarecrow outfit per team on a chair.
steps: First runner sprints to the chair and puts on EVERY piece of the outfit — shirt, pants, hat, gloves.
Strike a scarecrow pose (arms out!) and hold it for 3 seconds.
Sprint back and tag the next teammate, who runs up and puts the outfit on over their own clothes.
Keep going until every teammate has done the dress-up run.
First team finished wins — bonus cheer for the best scarecrow pose of the day.

variations.easier: Use fewer clothing pieces (just shirt and hat) for younger kids.
variations.harder: Add a straw-bale obstacle to run around, or require the pose to freeze until the team names it.

activities.safety: Clear the running lane of tripping hazards. Oversized pants get tucked or rolled so nobody trips.

activities.name: Costume Parade Freeze
activities.tagline: Parade your costume while the music plays — freeze in your best pose when it stops.

materials.item: room to parade in a circle

activities.setup: Clear a parade loop around the room. Line kids up in their costumes.
steps: Start the music — everyone parades the loop, showing off their costume.
When the music stops, FREEZE in your best costume pose.
The audience (everyone still frozen counts too) tries to guess each costume. Unfreeze one at a time to take a bow.
Music back on — parade again. Repeat 4–5 rounds.
End with a group freeze: the whole class holds one giant tableau pose.

variations.easier: Skip the guessing — just parade and freeze.
variations.harder: Add categories: freeze like your character would move, or pair up for duo poses.

activities.safety: Costumes need to let kids see and move safely — no vision-blocking masks while parading, and no real or toy weapons, ever.

activities.name: Pin the Hat on the Witch
activities.tagline: The party classic with a Halloween twist — blindfold, spin, stick the hat.

materials.item: a large witch face poster (drawn or printed)
tape or sticky tack on each hat
a soft scarf for a blindfold

activities.setup: Hang the witch poster at kid height. Put a tape loop on the back of each paper hat.
steps: One at a time, a kid stands a few steps back, gets gently blindfolded, and turns around once.
Walk forward slowly (a buddy can give 'left / right / straight' hints) and press the hat onto the poster.
Lift the blindfold — the room decides if the hat landed on the head or somewhere hilarious.
Everyone gets a turn. Closest hat to the head wins the round.
Leave the finished poster up as party decor.

variations.easier: Skip the blindfold — just stick the hat from a marked line.
variations.harder: Add decoy targets: also pin the broom, the cat, and the wart.

activities.safety: Clear the walking path of furniture and spot younger kids so nobody bumps into anything.

activities.name: Glow Stick Ring Toss
activities.tagline: Dim the lights and toss glowing rings onto bottle targets.

materials.item: sand or water to weight bottles

activities.setup: Crack the glow sticks to activate and connect the ends into rings. Weight the bottles, line them up, and dim the lights.
steps: Mark 2–3 throwing lines — closer for younger kids, farther for older.
Each kid gets 3 rings per turn. Toss underhand at the bottles.
Score: 1 point per ringer, 3 points for the farthest bottle.
Play 3 rounds, then a final 'sudden-death' round for the top scorers.
Collect all the rings at the end — they make great take-home party favors.

variations.easier: Use big floor targets (hula hoops) instead of bottles for easy wins.
variations.harder: Assign point values to each bottle and let kids keep a running score sheet.

activities.safety: Glow sticks are for tossing, not chewing or bending until they snap — any cracked stick goes straight in the trash.

activities.name: Pumpkin Roll Race
activities.tagline: Roll a pumpkin across the field with a pool noodle — no hands allowed.

materials.item: cones to mark lanes and a finish line

activities.setup: Set up straight lanes with cones, one pumpkin and one noodle per lane. Mark a clear finish line.
steps: Racers line up behind their pumpkins, noodle in hand.
On 'go', guide your pumpkin down the lane using ONLY the noodle — no hands, no feet.
If your pumpkin leaves your lane, roll it back in before continuing.
Run heats of 4–6 racers; winners race a final.
Cool-down: everyone helps carry pumpkins back. Losers' pumpkins get a consolation cheer.

variations.easier: Shorten the lane and let younger kids use their hands to roll.
variations.harder: Add slalom cones to weave around, or race in pairs with one noodle each.

activities.safety: Noodles guide pumpkins — never swing them at people. Pumpkins stay on the ground.

activities.name: Halloween Bingo
activities.tagline: Bingo with bats, pumpkins, and black cats — shout 'BOO!' instead of 'bingo'.

materials.item: printed Halloween bingo cards (or blank cards kids fill with Halloween drawings)
a caller set of picture cards or just call words aloud

activities.setup: Hand out cards and tokens. The caller needs the full list of Halloween words/pictures (ghost, bat, pumpkin, witch hat, spider, moon, candy, black cat, haunted house).
steps: The caller draws or announces one Halloween item at a time.
Kids cover the matching square on their card.
First to complete a row shouts 'BOO!' — check the card, then keep playing for blackout.
Winners get to be the caller for the next round.
Final round: everyone plays two cards at once for the championship.

variations.easier: Play with picture cards and matching (no reading needed) for younger kids.
variations.harder: Kids make their own cards by drawing 9 Halloween items in a grid — then swap cards and play.

activities.name: Candy Corn Estimation Jar
activities.tagline: Guess how many are in the jar — then count by tens to find out.

materials.item: a clear jar filled with candy corn (or dried beans for an allergy-safe version)

activities.setup: Fill the jar ahead of time and count the pieces as you fill (write the total down secretly). Set the jar where everyone can see it — no touching.
steps: Everyone studies the jar and writes down a guess on a slip — one guess each, no changing.
Collect the slips. Read a few guesses aloud — marvel at the range.
Pour out the jar and count together in groups of ten. Compare to the guesses.
Closest guess wins — the prize can be the honor of refilling the jar for the next class.
Talk strategy: who guessed by layers? By rows? What would you do differently next time?

variations.easier: Use a smaller jar and count by fives.
variations.harder: Fill two jars with different sizes of candy and estimate which holds more pieces.

activities.safety: Check allergies before any tasting happens — and keep the jar sealed until counting time if your class has food allergies.

activities.name: Costume Category Vote
activities.tagline: Everyone wins something when the categories are this creative.
activities.setup: Announce fun categories ahead of time: Most Creative, Funniest, Spookiest (Not Scary), Best Duo, Best Homemade. Set out ballots.
steps: Give everyone 5 minutes to look at all the costumes up close.
Everyone votes in each category — no voting for yourself.
Two volunteers tally the votes while the class does a costume parade.
Announce winners with a drumroll. Hand out paper medals.
Close by having every kid name one costume (not their own) they admired — everyone gets recognized.

variations.easier: Vote on just two categories to keep it short.
variations.harder: Let kids invent and campaign for their own new categories.

activities.safety: Categories stay kind — celebrate creativity and effort, never single anyone out.

activities.name: Ofrenda Memory Circle
activities.tagline: Build a small class ofrenda and share happy memories of people we miss.

materials.item: printed photos (optional — kids can also just bring a memory)

activities.setup: Set up the table with the cloth. Arrange marigolds and LED candles. Explain first: Día de los Muertos is a Mexican celebration where families honor loved ones who have died — building ofrendas with photos, marigolds, food, and candles to welcome their memory back. We're learning about it with respect.
steps: Each kid writes or draws a happy memory of someone they miss — a grandparent, a pet, anyone.
One at a time, kids may place their memory on the ofrenda and share it aloud — or just place it quietly. Passing is always okay.
Light the LED candles together as a symbol of remembrance.
Sit in a circle and share: what is one thing you learned from the person you remembered?
Leave the ofrenda up through the week. Take memories home on Friday.

variations.easier: The teacher builds the ofrenda and kids simply add drawings — no sharing aloud required.
variations.harder: Research real ofrenda elements (pan de muerto, sugar skulls, copal) and add labeled paper versions.

activities.safety: LED candles only — no real flames, ever. Sharing is always optional; some kids may prefer to listen.

activities.name: Coping Strategy Cards
activities.tagline: Kids build a personal deck of calm-down cards to keep in their desk.

materials.item: binder rings or yarn to bind the deck

activities.setup: Brainstorm calm-down strategies on the board first (deep breaths, count to ten, squeeze a stress ball, draw, ask for a break). Give each kid 4–5 blank cards.
steps: Each kid picks 4–5 strategies from the board and makes one card per strategy: draw a picture on one side, write the steps on the other.
Punch a hole in the corner of each card and bind them into a little flip deck.
Practice: the teacher names a tricky feeling, and kids flip to the card they'd use.
Keep the decks in desks or a calm corner. Kids can add new cards anytime.
Revisit in a month: which cards actually got used? Retire the duds, add new ideas.

variations.easier: Make just 2 cards with teacher-chosen strategies.
variations.harder: Kids design a 'help a friend' card: what to say when a classmate is upset.

activities.name: Kindness Poster Campaign
activities.tagline: Pairs design posters with one clear kindness message — then the hallways become the gallery.

materials.item: large paper or poster board (one per pair)

activities.setup: Pair kids up. Brainstorm what kindness actually looks like at school (including someone, using kind words, helping without being asked).
steps: Each pair picks ONE clear message — short enough to read from across the hall.
Design the poster: big readable letters, one strong image, the message front and center.
Present the poster to the class in 30 seconds: what does it say, and who is it for?
Hang the posters in hallways with permission — the campaign is the point.
A week later, walk the hall and notice: which posters do people stop to read?

variations.easier: Make small desk posters instead of hallway-sized ones.
variations.harder: Turn the best posters into a printed kindness calendar for the school office.

activities.name: Winter Joke Slam
activities.tagline: Everyone writes a clean winter joke — the applause-o-meter picks the champion.
activities.setup: Set the rules: winter-themed, clean, and kind — no jokes at anyone's expense. Hand out slips.
steps: Everyone writes one winter joke on a slip (a groaner is perfect) and drops it in the jar.
Shake the jar. Draw slips one at a time and read each joke aloud with full dramatic flair.
After each joke, the room rates it with applause — louder means funnier.
Top 3 joke-writers read their own jokes for the final round.
Crown the Winter Joke Champion. Post the winning joke on the board for the week.

variations.easier: The teacher reads pre-collected jokes instead of kids writing their own.
variations.harder: Kids illustrate the winning jokes into a class joke book.

activities.safety: Jokes stay kind — nothing that teases a person or group.

activities.name: Gratitude Door Decor
activities.tagline: The classroom door becomes a tree, and every kid hangs a leaf of thanks.

materials.item: butcher paper or a plastic tablecloth

activities.setup: Cover the classroom door (or a wall) with butcher paper and draw a big bare tree — trunk and branches. Cut or pre-cut paper leaves, one big leaf per kid.
steps: Each kid writes one thing they're grateful for on their leaf — specific beats generic ('my grandma's pancakes' beats 'food').
One at a time, kids tape their leaf onto the tree branches and read it aloud (or have the teacher read it).
Step back and admire: a bare tree turned full.
Leave it up through the season. Add new leaves anytime someone thinks of something.
Closing circle: which leaf on the tree surprised you most?

variations.easier: The teacher writes the gratitudes while kids decorate the leaves.
variations.harder: Make it a hallway installation: every class in the grade adds a tree to a 'gratitude forest'.

activities.name: Take-a-Stand Debate
activities.tagline: Agree or disagree? Stand on your side, give one reason, and switch if you're convinced.
activities.setup: Clear a line down the middle of the room: one side is AGREE, the other is DISAGREE. Prepare 4–6 low-stakes statements (e.g., 'Cereal is better than pancakes', 'Homework should be optional on Fridays').
steps: Read a statement aloud. Everyone stands on the AGREE or DISAGREE side — no middle.
Each side picks 2 speakers to give their best one-sentence reason.
After hearing both sides, anyone may switch sides. Movers say what convinced them.
New statement, everyone re-stands. Keep a brisk pace — 5 minutes per statement.
Debrief: which switch surprised you? What makes a reason convincing?

variations.easier: Use silly, zero-stakes statements and let kids give reasons in pairs instead of to the room.
variations.harder: Let kids write the statements, then run a formal version with opening statements and rebuttals.

activities.safety: Keep statements low-stakes and impersonal — no topics that single out a kid's life or beliefs.

activities.name: Poetry Share Circle
activities.tagline: Read poems aloud, steal your favorite line, and share why it stuck.

materials.item: a set of short printed poems (3–4 copies each of 5–6 poems)

activities.setup: Print a small stack of short, kid-friendly poems — funny ones work great. Lay them out like a menu.
steps: The teacher reads one poem aloud first, with feeling.
Everyone picks a poem, reads it silently twice, and underlines their favorite line.
Go around the circle: read your line aloud and say one sentence about why you picked it.
Second round (optional): anyone who wants to reads a whole poem aloud.
Exit ticket: write your own 4-line poem on any topic. No rhyming required.

variations.easier: The teacher reads all the poems and kids just pick a favorite line to repeat.
variations.harder: Host a poetry slam: volunteers perform a poem with gestures for the class.

activities.name: Pumpkin Letter Hunt
activities.tagline: Letters hide all over a pumpkin — find the one the teacher calls.

materials.item: letter stickers or masking tape with letters written on

activities.setup: Stick letter stickers all over the pumpkin — uppercase on one side, matching lowercase nearby. Set the pumpkin on a table everyone can reach.
steps: Gather the kids around the pumpkin. Name a letter out loud.
Kids take turns finding that letter on the pumpkin and pointing to it (or gently tapping it).
When they find it, everyone says the letter's sound together.
Level up: call out a letter and ask for a word that starts with it before the hunt continues.
End by singing the alphabet while pointing to letters around the pumpkin in order.

variations.easier: Use just 5–6 letters spaced far apart on the pumpkin.
variations.harder: Hide sight words instead of letters and have kids read the word they find.

activities.safety: Little hands can topple the pumpkin — keep it on a low, steady table.

activities.name: Secret Code Decoder Wheels
activities.tagline: Build a cipher wheel from cardstock, then trade coded messages to crack.

materials.item: cardstock or paper plates (2 circles per kid)

activities.setup: Cut two circles per kid: a big outer wheel and a smaller inner wheel (or use two paper plates, one trimmed smaller). Poke a center hole in each.
steps: Write the alphabet evenly around the outer wheel's edge.
Write the alphabet around the inner wheel's edge too, in a different color.
Pin the small wheel on top of the big one with the fastener — it should spin freely.
Learn the code: turn the inner wheel so A lines up under a different letter — that's your key. Write a message by finding each letter on the outer wheel and writing the inner-wheel letter beneath it.
Trade coded messages with a partner. Share only the key (which letter A lines up under) and decode each other's notes.

variations.easier: Use pre-made wheels where kids just decorate and practice with a given key.
variations.harder: Invent a symbol code (pictures instead of letters) or crack a message with an unknown key by guessing common letters.

activities.safety: Brass fasteners have a sharp point — the teacher pokes the center holes.

activities.name: Big-Feeling Scream Art
activities.tagline: Borrow the wavy style of a famous painting to draw your own big feeling.

materials.item: a printed image of Munch's 'The Scream' to look at together

activities.setup: Show the famous painting and talk about what you notice: the wavy lines, the bold colors, the huge feeling on the face. The rule: we're borrowing the STYLE, not copying the painting.
steps: Pick a big feeling you've had: excited, nervous, overjoyed, frustrated.
Draw a face showing that feeling — big and simple, filling the page.
Fill the background with wavy, swirly lines in bold colors, like the painting's sky.
Write one sentence under your art: what feeling is it, without telling the whole story.
Gallery walk: look at everyone's piece and guess the feeling. Artists reveal at the end.

variations.easier: Draw just the face with the wavy background — skip the sentence.
variations.harder: Make a diptych: the same scene drawn twice, once with calm straight lines and once with wild wavy ones.

activities.safety: Feelings are welcome; stories behind them stay private unless a kid chooses to share.

activities.name: Dinosaur Pattern Blocks
activities.tagline: Fill dino outlines with pattern blocks — geometry with teeth.

materials.item: printed dinosaur outline mats (or simple dino outlines drawn on paper)

activities.setup: Print or draw simple dinosaur silhouettes on paper — one per kid. Set out shared bins of pattern blocks.
steps: Pick a dinosaur mat and fill the outline with pattern blocks — match shapes to the spaces.
Count how many of each shape you used. Which shape did your dino need most?
Clear the mat and build the same dinosaur freehand, no outline.
Design your own dinosaur from blocks and name it. Draw it on paper so the design lasts.
Block museum: line up the paper designs and tour everyone's dinosaurs.

variations.easier: Use just 2–3 block shapes and a simple long-neck outline.
variations.harder: Measure your dinosaur in block-lengths, or build two dinos and compare their areas.

activities.name: Masterpiece Coloring Gallery
activities.tagline: Color famous artworks, write what you notice, and hang a class museum.

materials.item: printed coloring pages of famous artworks (several designs)

activities.setup: Print a variety of famous-artwork coloring pages — a few copies of each. Lay them out so kids can choose.
steps: Pick the artwork that catches your eye. Look at it for a full minute before coloring.
Color it your way — match the original colors or go wild, your choice.
Underneath, write one sentence: what do you notice in this artwork?
Hang every finished piece in a row — that's the class gallery.
Tour the gallery together. Each artist stands by their piece while the class shares one observation.

variations.easier: Color with no writing — just the gallery walk at the end.
variations.harder: Research the real painting behind your page and add a 3-fact label card.

activities.name: Continents Map Puzzle
activities.tagline: Cut out the seven continents and fit them onto a blank world map.

materials.item: printed world map outlines (one per kid)

activities.setup: Print a blank-ish world map (outlines only) and a sheet of labeled continent shapes per kid.
steps: Cut out the seven continents. Mix them up.
Fit each continent onto the map outline like a puzzle — no peeking at a finished map yet.
Glue them down, then label each one and color it a different color.
Partner quiz: cover the labels and name each continent by pointing.
Bonus: mark where you live, and draw a line to somewhere you'd love to visit.

variations.easier: Use pre-cut continents — just match, glue, and label.
variations.harder: Add the oceans, then research one animal from each continent and draw it on the map.

activities.safety: Scissors cut paper only.

activities.name: Homemade Christmas Ornaments
activities.tagline: Classic kid-made ornaments — keep some for your tree, gift the rest.

materials.item: clear plastic ornament balls or cardstock circles (one per kid)

activities.setup: Set up a decorating station with one ornament blank per kid and the decorations in shared bowls. Loop a ribbon hanger through each ornament first.
steps: Each kid picks an ornament blank and decorates it any way they like — glitter, stickers, painted dots, initials.
Let paint dry flat on a tray so it doesn't smudge.
Tie on the ribbon hanger and do a 'gallery walk' of everyone's tree.
Kids wrap one ornament to gift to someone and keep one for the classroom or family tree.

variations.easier: Pre-fill ornament balls with glitter so the littlest ones just shake and admire.
variations.harder: Try salt-dough cutouts (baked ahead) as the ornament base for a two-day project.

activities.safety: Glitter travels — cover the table and keep it out of eyes and mouths.

activities.name: Snowflake Paper Patterns
activities.tagline: Fold, snip, unfold — the six-fold surprise that never gets old.

materials.item: white printer paper or coffee filters (3 per kid)

activities.setup: Cut the paper into circles (or use coffee filters — they're already round and easy to fold).
steps: Fold each circle in half, then into thirds, so you get a six-fold wedge.
Snip triangles and curves out of the folded edges — not too close to the fold line.
Unfold and gasp. Hang the snowflakes on string across the windows.
Optional: tape two kids' snowflakes together back-to-back and notice no two match.

variations.easier: Pre-fold the wedges so little ones just cut the easy outer edges.
variations.harder: Challenge: try one cut too many and see what happens — then repair it with tape.

activities.safety: Scissors supervision; remind kids to cut away from fingers.

activities.name: Suet Cage Winter Feeder
activities.tagline: Pack a wire suet cage with winter bird food — a high-energy feast for cold days.

materials.item: wire suet cages (one per small group)

activities.setup: Set out bowls of shortening and dry ingredients. Put one suet cage and a length of string in front of each group.
steps: Mix two parts dry ingredients with one part softened shortening into a crumbly dough.
Pack the dough firmly into the suet cage — press it into every corner.
Thread string through the cage top and tie a strong hanger loop.
Hang the cages where birds can reach them but cats can't, and keep a visitor log.

variations.easier: Teacher mixes and packs; kids press the dough in with spoons.
variations.harder: Make two cages with different mixes (more oats vs. more seed) and compare visitors.

activities.safety: Shortening only — no peanut butter unless allergies are cleared. Wash hands after.

activities.name: Ice Ornaments
activities.tagline: Freeze water, leaves, and berries into hanging winter sun-catchers.

materials.item: natural bits: leaves, berries, pine sprigs

activities.setup: Lay out molds, a pitcher of water, and the natural bits. Cut string loops about 20 cm long, one per mold.
steps: Lay a string loop into each mold with the loop end hanging over the edge.
Arrange leaves, berries, and sprigs in the molds — flat is prettiest.
Fill each mold with water and set in the freezer overnight.
Pop the ornaments out and hang them outside. Watch what happens as they melt.

variations.easier: Teacher fills the molds; kids just arrange the nature bits.
variations.harder: Test variables: which ornaments melt fastest — sunny fence vs. shady porch?

activities.safety: No tasting the 'ingredients'; melt water goes on the garden, not in mouths.

activities.name: Hanukkah Counting Chain
activities.tagline: A paper chain of eight links plus a leader — a craft for learning how Hanukkah counts its eight nights.
activities.setup: Cut paper into strips (about 3 × 20 cm), eight of one color and one of another for the leader link. Frame the activity as learning about a holiday other families celebrate — this is a counting craft, not a ceremony.
steps: Chain the eight links together, one for each night of Hanukkah.
Add the leader link at the front of the chain.
On each link, write something the group has learned about the holiday.
Hang the chain and add one fact per day as a class countdown.

variations.easier: Teacher assembles the chain; kids decorate the links with drawings.
variations.harder: Research one more true fact per night from a reliable source and add it.

activities.safety: Cultural note: this craft is for learning about Hanukkah, not performing it. Treat the holiday with respect — ask, don't assume, about anyone's traditions.

activities.name: Kwanzaa Unity Garland
activities.tagline: A red, black, and green garland made while learning about Kwanzaa's seven principles — a values craft, not a ceremony.

materials.item: red, black, and green construction paper

activities.setup: Cut paper into strips. Frame the activity as learning about Kwanzaa — a week-long celebration of family, community, and culture — and its seven principles (the Nguzo Saba). This is a classroom craft about its values, not a ceremony.
steps: Cut strips of red, black, and green paper.
On each strip, write one of the seven principles (unity, self-determination, collective work, cooperative economics, purpose, creativity, faith).
Link the strips into a garland, alternating the three colors.
Read the garland together and discuss: what does each principle look like in our classroom?

variations.easier: Use fewer strips (three colors, one word each: unity, creativity, faith).
variations.harder: Research what each principle means in practice and add an example to each strip.

activities.safety: Cultural note: this craft is for learning about Kwanzaa, not performing it. Present it as a values celebration some families observe; keep the tone respectful.

activities.name: Snowball Toss Math
activities.tagline: Toss indoor snowballs into point buckets — arithmetic with your whole body.

materials.item: soft indoor snowballs (crumpled paper or yarn balls, 2 per kid)

activities.setup: Line up the point buckets along one wall, a few feet from the throw line. Give every kid two snowballs. Post a score chart.
steps: Each kid throws both snowballs into the buckets and adds their points.
After everyone has thrown, kids compute their running totals.
Round two: teams throw and pool their points — first team to 100 wins.
Close with the 'blizzard round': everyone throws at once, then the class sorts and counts every bucket together.

variations.easier: Use buckets labeled 1 and 2 only; count together on fingers.
variations.harder: Add a multiplier bucket: a snowball in the star bucket doubles your round.

activities.safety: Throw underhand only, and only toward the buckets — no aiming at people.

activities.name: Animal Walk Relay
activities.tagline: Waddle like a penguin, stomp like a polar bear — a relay across the gym floor.

materials.item: cones or tape to mark the relay line

activities.setup: Split the group into equal teams behind the start line. Name three winter animal walks and demo each one.
steps: Leg 1: penguin waddle (heels together, arms at sides, wobble to the cone and back).
Leg 2: polar-bear prowl (bear crawl — hands and feet, knees off the floor).
Leg 3: arctic-hare hop (two-footed hops all the way).
Leg 4: snowy-owl swoop (arms out, slow flapping glide). First team sitting in a line when their last runner returns wins.

variations.easier: One animal walk per round instead of four legs; everyone does the same one.
variations.harder: Add a 'blizzard obstacle': teammates crawl under a held-up blanket halfway.

activities.safety: Clear the floor of anything slippery first; no running full speed on tile.

activities.name: Winter Freeze Dance
activities.tagline: Freeze dance with a twist: when the music stops, the caller shouts a winter animal.
activities.setup: You need nothing but music and space to move. Assign a caller (rotate the job).
steps: Everyone dances while the music plays.
Music stops — everyone freezes, and the caller shouts a winter animal: 'penguin!', 'polar bear!', 'snowy owl!'
Everyone holds the pose of that animal until the music restarts.
Rotate callers every few rounds; the silliest-held pose wins applause.

variations.easier: Caller gives extra time to find the pose; no one sits out for a wrong guess.
variations.harder: Add 'migrating goose': kids link up in a V and glide to a new spot in the room.

activities.safety: Keep dance space clear of furniture corners; freeze means stop, not crash.

activities.name: Year-in-Review Quilt
activities.tagline: Every kid decorates one paper square with their year's highlight — together they become a class quilt.

materials.item: paper squares (one per kid, same size)
a large backing sheet or bulletin board

activities.setup: Cut identical paper squares (about 20 cm). Set out art supplies in shared caddies and lay the backing sheet flat.
steps: Each kid fills one square with their year's highlight — a drawing, a word, a photo corner, a tiny collage.
Kids share their square with the table and explain what it means.
Assemble the squares edge-to-edge on the backing sheet, alternating light and dark colors for a real quilt feel.
Hang the quilt where families can see it at the New Year event or open house.

variations.easier: Draw the highlight; teacher writes the caption the child dictates.
variations.harder: Leave one blank square per kid to fill in June — the quilt grows all year.

activities.safety: Highlights are self-chosen — nobody has to explain anything they'd rather keep private.

activities.name: Resolution Ladder
activities.tagline: New Year goals as a ladder — one small, doable rung per month.

materials.item: a large ladder drawn on butcher paper

activities.setup: Draw a big ladder on butcher paper with 12 rungs. Give each kid 12 strips.
steps: Each kid writes one small, doable goal on each strip — one per month.
Goals must be concrete: 'read 10 minutes daily' beats 'read more'.
Tape the strips onto the rungs, grouped by month, and hang the ladder up.
Revisit monthly: flip over the rungs you hit and set the next month's.

variations.easier: Do 4 seasons instead of 12 months; draw the goal instead of writing it.
variations.harder: Add a 'stretch rung' at the top: one big dream goal for the whole year.

activities.safety: Goals are private to share — kids post only what they want to post.

activities.name: Midnight Countdown Rehearsal
activities.tagline: A practice New Year's Eve: chant the 10-to-0 countdown and cheer in a brand-new pretend year.
activities.setup: No setup needed. This works great as the last 15 minutes before a winter break dismissal.
steps: Everyone stands in a circle. The leader announces what 'year' we're cheering in.
Count down from 10 together, getting louder each number.
At zero: cheer, clap, and do a group jump — the new 'year' has arrived.
Go around the circle: each kid names one thing they're glad happened this year.
Optional finale: countdown in a whisper, then a tiny silent cheer.

variations.easier: Count down from 5 instead of 10; skip the go-around for big groups.
variations.harder: Let kids run the countdown in another language the class is learning.

activities.safety: Mind the volume if another class is next door — schedule accordingly.

activities.name: Track Prints Detective
activities.tagline: Find animal prints in snow or mud, match them to a chart, solve the mystery.

materials.item: a camera or phone for photos

activities.setup: After fresh snow or rain, scout a route with visible prints. Print one track chart per pair.
steps: Walk the route quietly and look for prints — snow and mud both work.
Photograph each set of prints and note where you found them.
Match them against the ID chart: how many toes, claw marks or not, size?
Log the 'case file': what animal, how many, which direction, and the evidence that convinced you.

variations.easier: Teacher pre-prints photo cards of three local tracks; kids match at the site.
variations.harder: Measure stride length between prints and estimate the animal's speed.

activities.safety: Stay on paths; don't follow prints into streets or private yards.

activities.name: Frost Observation
activities.tagline: Magnify the ice crystals on windows and leaves and sketch their patterns.
activities.setup: On a frosty morning, find windows, car hoods (with the owner's okay), or leaves with visible frost. Hand out magnifiers and sketch paper.
steps: Look at the frost through the magnifier — find the six-pointed crystals.
Sketch three different crystals you actually see, not what you imagine.
Compare sketches: does everyone's frost look the same? Different?
Discuss: what did the night have to be like for this frost to form?

variations.easier: One shared magnifier, teacher narrates; kids draw one big crystal together.
variations.harder: Check the overnight low online and connect it to how feathery the frost is.

activities.safety: Don't lick frosty metal, and don't touch anyone's car without permission.

activities.name: Bark and Branch Study
activities.tagline: Identify winter trees with no leaves — bark patterns and buds are the clues.

materials.item: a winter tree ID key (printed or one shared book)
paper and crayons for bark rubbings

activities.setup: Pick a park or schoolyard with a few different trees. Print one ID key per pair.
steps: Do bark rubbings: press paper against the trunk, rub sideways with a crayon.
Study the buds at branch tips with the ID key — shape, size, arrangement.
Match each tree to the key and label your rubbings with the tree's name.
Back inside: line up the rubbings and see if the class agrees on each ID.

variations.easier: Focus on just two trees; teacher does the ID, kids do the rubbings.
variations.harder: Keep a winter tree log through the season and watch the buds swell in spring.

activities.safety: Don't pull bark off trees or break branches — rubbings only.

activities.name: Dissolving Warm-Drink Lab
activities.tagline: Hot cocoa science: does powder dissolve faster in hot water or cold?
activities.setup: Set up two stations: warm water and cold water. Give each pair two clear cups, one spoon of cocoa mix, and a sugar cube.
steps: Predict: which cup dissolves the cocoa faster — warm or cold? Write it down.
Add the cocoa to both cups at the same time. Time how long each takes to fully dissolve with the same stirring.
Repeat with the sugar cubes — but this time, one cup stirred, one not.
Chart the class results. Discuss: why did the warm water win?

variations.easier: Teacher runs the demo up front; kids just predict and watch.
variations.harder: Try milk vs. water, or test whether crushed vs. whole sugar cube matters.

activities.safety: Water should be warm, not hot — an adult handles the kettle. Check for dairy allergies if tasting.

activities.name: Temperature Melt Race
activities.tagline: Three cups of water, three ice cubes — predict which melts first, then watch.
activities.setup: Set out the three water temperatures labeled A, B, C (don't reveal which is which yet). Give each pair three cups and three ice cubes.
steps: Each pair predicts the melt order and writes it down — no changing it.
Drop one ice cube in each cup at the same time and start the timer.
Record the exact melt time for each cube.
Reveal the temperatures. Who predicted right? Discuss what heat does to ice.

variations.easier: Run it as a teacher demo; kids predict by holding up fingers (1, 2, 3).
variations.harder: Add a fourth cup with salt in the ice water — does salt change the melt?

activities.safety: An adult pours the warm water. Dry spills immediately so nobody slips.

activities.name: Snowflake Mirror
activities.tagline: Pairs mirror each other's snowflake arm poses — then try to catch the change.
activities.setup: No setup at all. Pair the kids up, facing each other, arms' length apart.
steps: One partner is the 'snowflake', the other is the 'mirror'.
The snowflake slowly moves arms and body into a new pose; the mirror copies in real time.
After a minute, swap roles.
Round two: the mirror has to spot three deliberate changes the snowflake sneaks in.
Close: each pair shows their best snowflake pose to the group.

variations.easier: Whole group mirrors the teacher instead of pairing up.
variations.harder: Three-person teams: one caller shouts pose words ('branch!', 'crystal!').

activities.name: Winter Tall Tale
activities.tagline: A circle story where every kid adds one wild winter sentence.
activities.setup: Nothing needed — just a circle. The teacher starts the story with one sentence.
steps: Teacher: 'On the coldest morning of the year, I opened my door and saw...'
Each kid adds exactly one sentence, building on the last one.
Encourage wild but connected additions — the yeti borrowed the bus, the snow spoke back.
After one full circle, the teacher closes the tale in three sentences.
Optional: vote on the best sentence and start a new tale with it.

variations.easier: Kids can pass, or just add a sound effect instead of a sentence.
variations.harder: Two circles compete for the best ending, then swap and judge.

activities.name: Warm-Up Countdown
activities.tagline: Call-and-response counting with jumping jacks — math that warms the room.
activities.setup: Push desks back so everyone has arm room. Teacher leads the first round.
steps: Teacher calls a number and a move: 'Ten jumping jacks — go!' The group counts aloud together while doing it.
Rotate the caller: each kid picks the next number and move (high knees, arm circles, toe touches).
Add math: 'Seven minus two jumping jacks — how many?' Solve, then do them.
Final round: count down from 20 to 1 together, getting quieter each number, ending seated.

variations.easier: Just counting with claps, no big moves; teacher picks every number.
variations.harder: Add multiplication: 'Three sets of four arm circles — how many total?'

activities.safety: Moves stay low-impact near furniture; anyone can march in place instead.

activities.name: Paper Mitten Match
activities.tagline: Decorate mitten pairs, mix them up, and play memory across the room.
activities.setup: Cut out pairs of paper mittens ahead of time (trace one hand shape and flip it). Give each kid two matching mittens.
steps: Each kid decorates their two mittens identically — same pattern, same colors.
Collect one mitten from every kid into the paper bag and hide the other halves.
Scatter the hidden mittens face-down on the rug; kids draw a mitten from the bag.
One at a time, each kid flips a rug mitten trying to find their pair's match. Matched pairs hang on the 'clothesline' to dry.

variations.easier: Teacher matches for them: hold up two mittens, 'same or different?'
variations.harder: Three-mitten sets: decorate a trio and match all three.

activities.safety: No running while searching — walk to the rug.

activities.name: Winter Wreath Collage
activities.tagline: A paper-plate wreath layered with cut-paper greens — a winter door classic.
activities.setup: Cut the centers out of the paper plates ahead of time so they're rings. Put green paper scraps in shared bowls.
steps: Glue torn or cut green paper pieces all around the ring, overlapping like leaves.
Add red paper berries (tiny circles) and a ribbon bow at the top.
Write the child's name and the year on the back.
Hang the wreaths on the classroom door for the season.

variations.easier: Teacher pre-cuts leaf shapes; kids just glue them around the ring.
variations.harder: Weave in real pressed leaves between the paper layers for texture.

activities.safety: Scissors supervision; glue sticks, not bottles, for the little ones.

activities.name: Cotton-Ball Penguin
activities.tagline: A fluffy cotton-ball penguin puppet with real googly attitude.

materials.item: black and white paper ovals (one set per kid)

activities.setup: Pre-cut the black body ovals and white belly ovals. Put cotton balls, eyes, and beaks in shared bowls.
steps: Glue the white belly oval onto the black body oval.
Glue cotton balls all around the edge for a fluffy outline.
Add googly eyes and the orange beak.
Give your penguin a name and introduce it to a neighbor's penguin.

variations.easier: Teacher glues the body together; kids stick on cotton balls and eyes.
variations.harder: Add flippers (small black paper wings) and a paper ice floe to stand on.

activities.safety: Googly eyes are small — keep them out of mouths; supervision for under-5s.

activities.name: Arctic Animal Research Jigsaw
activities.tagline: Small expert teams research one arctic animal each, then teach the class.

materials.item: arctic animal fact sheets (one animal per team: polar bear, arctic fox, snowy owl, narwhal, penguin, seal)

activities.setup: Prepare one simple fact sheet per animal (diet, habitat, one superpower adaptation). Split the class into expert teams of 3–4.
steps: Each team studies its animal's sheet and picks the three coolest facts.
Teams make a poster: drawing, the three facts, and one question for the class.
New mixed groups form with one expert from each animal — each expert teaches their animal in two minutes.
Back together: the class votes on the most surprising adaptation learned.

variations.easier: Teacher reads the fact sheet aloud; teams draw the animal and dictate one fact.
variations.harder: Add a 'myth vs. fact' round: teams invent one plausible-sounding fake fact and the class guesses which is fake.

activities.name: Gingerbread Shape Build
activities.tagline: Engineer the tallest tower you can from graham crackers and icing 'mortar'.
activities.setup: Give each pair a plate, a stack of graham crackers, and a squeeze bottle of icing. Set a 20-minute build timer.
steps: Plan first: sketch the tower on the plate's edge before touching food.
Build with icing as mortar — let each layer set a minute before adding more.
Measure the finished tower; the tallest standing tower wins.
Decorate, photograph, and then — the best part — eat the engineering.

variations.easier: Build flat houses (walls only) instead of tall towers.
variations.harder: Test shapes: which holds more weight, a cube tower or a pyramid?

activities.safety: Check for wheat, dairy, and egg allergies before anyone eats. Icing is sticky — wash hands and wipe tables after.

activities.name: Tissue Paper Cherry Blossoms
activities.tagline: Twisted paper branches covered in pink tissue blooms — spring on a branch.

materials.item: brown paper strips or twisted newspaper

activities.setup: Set out one brown paper strip per kid and piles of pre-cut tissue squares (about 2 inches). Put a dab station of glue at each table.
steps: Twist each brown strip tightly into a branch — thicker at the bottom, forked at the top.
Take one tissue square, pinch it in the center, and twist the pinched end. That is one blossom.
Glue 8 to 12 blossoms along each branch, clustering 2 or 3 together for fullness. Mix pink and white.
Glue the finished branch onto blue construction paper so the blossoms pop.
Gallery walk: line the branches up and spot whose tree looks windiest.

variations.easier: Pre-cut the tissue squares and let little ones just pinch and stick.
variations.harder: Shade the blossoms: layer a small white twist inside a larger pink one.

activities.safety: Scissors supervision; remind kids to cut away from fingers.

activities.name: Coffee Filter Butterflies
activities.tagline: Markers plus a spritz of water turn a coffee filter into butterfly wings.

materials.item: round basket coffee filters (2 per kid)

activities.setup: Give each kid two coffee filters and markers. Fill spray bottles with plain water — one per table.
steps: Color a coffee filter all over with washable markers — the brighter the better. Patterns beat solid color.
Lay the filter flat and spritz it lightly: two pumps, not a soak. Watch the colors bleed together.
Let it dry for 5 minutes (wave it gently to speed things up).
Pinch the dry filter in the middle and clip it with a clothespin — that is the butterfly body.
Wrap a pipe cleaner around the clothespin top and curl the ends into antennae. Two filters make a four-wing butterfly.

variations.easier: The teacher does the spritzing; kids only color and pinch.
variations.harder: Design challenge: make both wings symmetrical, then make a pair that is deliberately mismatched.

activities.safety: Washable markers only; spray bottles pointed at the paper, never at faces.

activities.name: Painted Rock Ladybugs
activities.tagline: Smooth rocks from the yard become ladybugs — then hide them for others to find.

materials.item: red and black paint or paint pens

activities.setup: Collect smooth, flat rocks ahead of time — about the size of a cookie. Wash and dry them. Cover tables with newspaper.
steps: Paint each rock red all over and let it dry completely.
Paint a black half-circle at one end for the head.
Add black dots down the back — no two ladybugs need the same pattern.
Dot two tiny white eyes on the head.
Optional: hide the finished ladybugs around the schoolyard for other classes to discover.

variations.easier: The teacher paints the red base coat ahead; kids add dots and faces.
variations.harder: Make a 'habitat card' for each ladybug: where the rock was found and what real ladybugs eat there.

activities.safety: Wash hands after handling rocks and paint. Smocks or old shirts — the paint does not wash out.

activities.name: Pressed Flower Bookmarks
activities.tagline: Real pressed flowers sealed into a bookmark — a spring keepsake that lasts.

materials.item: small fresh flowers and leaves (picked with permission)
clear packing tape or contact paper

activities.setup: Pressing takes days, so start a class pressing book at least 3 days ahead (or keep one going all spring). Cut cardstock into bookmark strips and set out tape.
steps: Open the pressing book and let each kid choose 3 to 5 flat, dry flowers or leaves.
Arrange them on a cardstock strip — leave a border all around.
Cover the whole strip with a smooth layer of clear packing tape, pressing out bubbles.
Trim the tape edges, punch a hole at the top, and tie a yarn tassel.
Write your name and the date on the back — a real keepsake.

variations.easier: Use a pre-pressed class set so little ones only arrange and tape.
variations.harder: Label each flower on the back with its name — turn it into a botany card.

activities.safety: Pick only flowers you are allowed to pick, and never taste any plant. Wash hands after.

activities.name: Egg Carton Tulip Garden
activities.tagline: Cut-up egg cartons bloom into a whole tray of painted tulips.
activities.setup: Cut the egg cartons into individual cups ahead of time (one per kid, plus spares). Poke a small hole in the bottom of each cup.
steps: Paint the outside of your cup a bright petal color and let it dry.
Push a green pipe cleaner up through the hole — that is the stem. Bend the top so the cup does not slide off.
Glue a pom-pom or tissue ball inside the cup for the flower center.
Cut two leaf shapes from green paper and glue them to the stem.
Plant all the tulips upright in the group tray — a full spring garden by the end of class.

variations.easier: Pre-cut the cups and pre-poke the holes; little ones just paint and assemble.
variations.harder: Painting challenge: make a bud (cup pinched shut), a bloom, and a fading flower — the three stages of spring.

activities.safety: Scissors are for the teacher's prep step only; remind kids to keep paint off clothes.

activities.name: Paper Plate Sunflower
activities.tagline: A paper plate, some yellow paint, and a seed-mosaic center — instant sunflower.

materials.item: brown tissue paper or real sunflower seeds (for gluing)

activities.setup: Hand out one paper plate per kid and put the yellow paint or crayons in the middle of each table.
steps: Color the whole plate yellow — paint is brightest, crayons work too.
Cut slits all around the plate edge (about an inch deep) and bend every other flap slightly down: those are the petals.
Glue brown tissue scraps or real seeds in a circle in the middle for the flower head.
Glue a green paper strip to the back as the stem.
Hold them up together — a field of sunflowers, zero watering needed.

variations.easier: Use crayons instead of paint for zero drying time.
variations.harder: Two-tone challenge: paint the petal tips a darker yellow-orange gradient.

activities.name: Worm Weather Watch
activities.tagline: After rain, the worms come out — count them, log the weather, find the pattern.
activities.setup: Best the morning after rain. Mark one observation square per pair with chalk or string — about a beach-towel size patch of grass or pavement edge.
steps: Spend 5 quiet minutes just watching your square. Count every worm you see.
Log the weather: temperature guess, cloudy or sunny, ground wet or dry.
Watch one worm for 2 full minutes. Which way does it move? How?
Gently return any handled worms to the soil where you found them.
Back inside, chart the class counts against the weather log. Do rainy mornings really mean more worms?

variations.easier: One big class square that everyone watches together.
variations.harder: Keep the log for two weeks and graph worm counts against actual rainfall.

activities.safety: Wash hands after. Handle worms gently and put them back — never take them inside, and do not dig up garden beds.

activities.name: Puddle Depth Gauge
activities.tagline: Mark a stick, measure the puddle, come back later — where did the water go?

materials.item: paint stir sticks or dowels (one per pair)

activities.setup: Needs a real puddle — right after rain is perfect. Give each pair a stick, a ruler, and a marker.
steps: Mark centimeter lines up one side of your stick with the ruler and marker.
Pick a puddle. Measure the depth at the center and at two edges — write all three numbers down.
Predict: in one hour, will the puddle be deeper, shallower, or gone?
Come back in an hour and measure the same three spots.
Compare: which spot shrank fastest? Sunny puddles vs. shady ones — who wins the evaporation race?

variations.easier: One class puddle, one class stick, group predictions.
variations.harder: Calculate the depth lost per hour and predict when the puddle vanishes — then check tomorrow.

activities.safety: Measure from the puddle's edge — no wading into deep water, and stay out of streets and parking lots.

activities.name: Flower Part Dissect
activities.tagline: Take a flower apart piece by piece and find the machinery inside.

materials.item: one large flower per pair (tulip or lily from the grocery store)

activities.setup: Buy the flowers the same day — tulips and lilies have big, easy-to-find parts. Give each pair one flower, a plate, and tweezers.
steps: Draw your flower whole first — you will want the 'before' picture.
Pull off the petals one by one and lay them in a row. Count them.
Find the stamens (the stalks with powdery tips) — touch the pollen with a fingertip. That powder is the point of the whole flower.
Find the pistil in the center — the sticky-tipped stalk. That is where seeds begin.
Tape each part onto a labeled diagram: petal, sepal, stamen, pistil.

variations.easier: The teacher dissects one flower up front while kids label along.
variations.harder: Compare two different flowers side by side — which parts match, which do not?

activities.safety: Check for pollen or flower allergies before starting. No tasting any part. Wash hands when done.

activities.name: Nest Material Challenge
activities.tagline: Build a bird nest from yard scraps — then test it with a marble egg.

materials.item: a marble or small ball per team as the 'egg'

activities.setup: Set a 10-minute collection window and clear boundaries for gathering: twigs, grass, leaves, and mud only — nothing from living plants.
steps: Teams of 3 get 10 minutes to gather nest materials — no raiding real nests.
Build time: 15 minutes to weave a nest that can hold the marble egg.
Test 1: set the marble in and count to 10. Still in? Pass.
Test 2: the gentle shake — lift the nest 6 inches and wobble it. Egg stays? Sturdy nest.
Test 3 (optional): the drop — knee height onto grass. Survivors get bragging rights.
Debrief: which materials gripped best? Real birds figured this out without hands.

variations.easier: Build on a paper plate base so the nest has a head start.
variations.harder: Blind materials round: each team draws 3 material cards and may only use those.

activities.safety: Build nests only — never touch a real nest or egg. Watch for thorns and wash hands after handling mud.

activities.name: Seed Dispersal Design
activities.tagline: Maple seeds spin — design a paper seed that stays airborne even longer.

materials.item: maple seeds if you can find them

activities.setup: If maple seeds are around, start by dropping a few and watching them spin. Set a drop zone: same chair or stair height for every test, floor clear below.
steps: Fold the classic paper helicopter: cut a strip, slit the top, fold the blades opposite ways.
Drop it from the test height three times. Time each fall — average it.
Now redesign: longer blades? Heavier bottom? Wider wings? Change ONE thing at a time.
Test each design three times and record. Longest average flight wins.
Final round: tape a paper clip 'seed' to your design as payload. Does it still fly?

variations.easier: Everyone builds the same basic helicopter and just races flight times.
variations.harder: Constraint cards: must spin clockwise, must land within a hula hoop, must carry two paper clips.

activities.safety: Keep the drop zone clear — nobody walks under the testing chair.

activities.name: Sprout Growth Race
activities.tagline: Two cups, one seed each, different light — place your bets on the sprout.
activities.setup: Set up a soil station with scoops. Pre-label cups 'SUN' and 'DARK' for younger kids to save time.
steps: Fill two cups with soil, poke one bean an inch deep in each, water both.
Label them and place one on a sunny windowsill, one in a dark cupboard.
Everyone predicts: which sprouts first? Write it down — no changing bets.
Water lightly every other day and measure any growth with a ruler.
After a week, compare. The dark cup usually sprouts first — but which one looks healthier? Discuss why.

variations.easier: One class pair of cups that everyone watches together.
variations.harder: Add a third cup: watered vs. never watered — which variable matters more?

activities.safety: Wash hands after handling soil. Soil stays in the cups, not on faces.

activities.name: Bubble Snake Blower
activities.tagline: A sock, a bottle, and some soapy water — blow a bubble snake a foot long.

materials.item: plastic bottles with the bottoms cut off (teacher preps)
dish soap and water in shallow trays

activities.setup: Cut the bottoms off the bottles ahead of time — no kid cutting plastic. Mix a good squirt of dish soap into each tray of water.
steps: Stretch a sock tightly over the cut end of the bottle and rubber-band it on.
Dip the sock end into the soapy tray — soak it well.
Blow gently through the mouthpiece. Out comes a long, wiggly bubble snake.
Experiment: fast blow vs. slow blow — which makes the longer snake?
Longest-snake contest: measure the winner with a ruler.

variations.easier: The teacher does the dipping; kids only blow.
variations.harder: Two-sock challenge: does a double layer make bigger or smaller bubbles? Hypothesize first.

activities.safety: Blow, do not suck — and keep the soapy water out of eyes. Wash hands after.

activities.name: Evaporation Chalk Lines
activities.tagline: Trace the puddle with chalk, wait an hour, and watch the water lose.
activities.setup: Needs puddles and pavement — right after rain on the blacktop is ideal. Give each pair a piece of chalk.
steps: Pick a puddle and trace its exact edge with chalk. Write the time next to your line.
Predict: in 30 minutes, will your line be inside or outside the water?
Come back in 30 minutes and trace the new edge in a different color.
Repeat at 60 minutes if you have time.
Compare lines: sunny-side puddles vs. shady ones. Where did the water go? (Up! Into the air.)

variations.easier: One class puddle, two tracings, group discussion.
variations.harder: Copy your puddle outlines onto graph paper and estimate the area lost.

activities.safety: Chalk on pavement only — not walls or cars. Stay on dry edges, out of the street.

activities.name: Sponge Bucket Relay
activities.tagline: Soak, sprint, squeeze — the relay where the water does the traveling.
activities.setup: Set two lanes: a full water bucket at the start of each, an empty bucket about 30 feet away. One sponge per team.
steps: Teams line up behind their water bucket.
First runner soaks the sponge, runs to the far bucket, squeezes it in, runs back, and hands off.
Next runner goes. No wringing the sponge out early — it has to travel wet.
First team to fill their far bucket to the marked line wins.
Losers' consolation: everyone gets to dump the leftover water on the grass.

variations.easier: Shorten the lane to 15 feet for little legs.
variations.harder: Overhead carry: the sponge must travel above your head — drips count against you.

activities.safety: Wet pavement is slippery — walk the turn at the far bucket, no diving stops. Shoes stay on.

activities.name: Puddle Stomp Parade
activities.tagline: Line up, chant, and stomp every puddle on the route — rhythm required.
activities.setup: No setup — just rain boots or old shoes and a route with puddles. Scout the route first for anything deeper than a shoe.
steps: Line up single file behind the leader.
March to a chant: 'Stomp, stomp, puddle stomp!' — leader calls, group answers.
Every puddle on the route gets stomped in rhythm as the line passes through.
Rotate the leader every two puddles — new leaders invent new verses.
Grand finale: everyone finds the biggest puddle and does one giant synchronized stomp. Then shake off and head in.

variations.easier: Skip the chant — just stomp freely through the puddles.
variations.harder: Kids compose the verses: each puddle gets its own rhyming couplet.

activities.safety: Rain boots or shoes you do not mind soaking. Splash-zone rule: no stomping right next to someone's face.

activities.name: Spring Sound Map
activities.tagline: Sit still for two minutes, then draw every sound you heard — and where it lived.
activities.setup: No materials — this one runs on ears. Set clear sit-spot boundaries first, spaced so nobody distracts a neighbor.
steps: Everyone finds a sit spot and gets comfortable.
Eyes closed, two full minutes of just listening. No talking, no peeking.
Open eyes. On paper (or in the air with a finger), draw an X for yourself.
Mark every sound you heard around the X: bird up-left, wind overhead, car far right — closer sounds closer to the X.
Share: who heard the most sounds? Who heard something nobody else did?
Optional: come back tomorrow at the same time and compare maps.

variations.easier: Skip the drawing — just list the sounds out loud after.
variations.harder: Layer it: mark human sounds with circles and nature sounds with stars.

activities.name: Puddle Hopscotch
activities.tagline: Classic hopscotch with a twist: the blue squares are puddles — jump them.

materials.item: a small stone per kid as a marker

activities.setup: Draw a standard hopscotch court on pavement. Color 2 or 3 squares solid blue — those are the puddles.
steps: Toss your marker onto square one and hop the court as usual.
Rule: you may never land in a blue puddle square — jump clean over it.
Land in a puddle and you lose your turn (and get pretend-soaked).
Finish the court, then toss to square two. First to complete all throws wins.
Remix round: players take turns adding a new blue puddle square.

variations.easier: Let little ones step around the puddles instead of jumping them.
variations.harder: Double-puddle jump: two blue squares in a row — only for confident hoppers.

activities.safety: Chalk on pavement only. Keep the court clear of bikes and foot traffic.

activities.name: Egg Roll Race
activities.tagline: The egg-and-spoon classic, spring edition — plastic eggs, real competition.
activities.setup: Set two lanes with a turnaround cone about 20 feet out. One spoon and one plastic egg per racer.
steps: Racers balance the egg on the spoon — one hand on the spoon, other hand behind your back.
On 'go', walk (then run, for older kids) to the cone, circle it, and come back.
Drop the egg? Stop, pick it up, put it back on the spoon, keep going.
Tag the next teammate's hand for the relay handoff.
Winning team picks the victory chant. Losing team picks it too — everyone chants it.

variations.easier: Carry the egg in your hand instead of on the spoon.
variations.harder: Spoon-in-mouth round for older kids — no hands allowed at all.

activities.safety: Clear the lane of tripping hazards. No running with the spoon in the mouth for the youngest racers.

activities.name: Jellybean Sort Graph
activities.tagline: Sort the jellybeans, count the colors, graph it — then check your prediction.

materials.item: jellybeans or colored counters (one small cup per pair)

activities.setup: Portion one small cup of jellybeans per pair — mixed colors. Hand out graph paper with the color labels pre-written for younger kids.
steps: Before opening: predict which color you will have the most of. Write it down.
Sort your cup by color into the muffin tin.
Count each color and write the numbers down.
Build a bar graph: one bar per color, one square per bean.
Compare: did your prediction win? Combine the class data — does the big graph match anyone's small one?

variations.easier: Sort and count only — skip the graph.
variations.harder: Fractions: what fraction of your cup is red? Convert the graph to percentages.

activities.safety: Allergy check before any tasting, and set the eat-or-not rule before the cups open — not halfway through.

activities.name: Easter Egg Catapult
activities.tagline: Popsicle sticks, rubber bands, one plastic spoon — launch the egg at the target.
